Newborn Care

How to Swaddle a Baby Safely and When to Stop

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited by Mohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama — checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

To swaddle a baby safely, wrap a thin blanket snugly around the arms and chest, keep the wrap loose around the hips and knees, leave the face fully uncovered, and always place your baby on their back to sleep. Done that way, swaddling is considered acceptable by mainstream pediatric guidance, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, and it helps many newborns settle. It also comes with an end date: you stop at the very first sign your baby is trying to roll, often by around 2 months.

Why swaddling calms newborns

Newborns spend nine months held snugly on all sides, so the wide open feeling of a crib can be startling. A good swaddle recreates some of that gentle, even pressure. It also softens the startle reflex, the sudden arm fling that jolts many young babies awake just as they drift off. For lots of newborns, that combination means easier settling, longer stretches of calm, and less frantic crying in the first weeks. Not every baby agrees. Some squirm, grunt, and fight the wrap from day one, and that is normal too. Swaddling is one soothing option among several, not a requirement for good sleep.

The American Academy of Pediatrics considers swaddling acceptable when it is done correctly: baby on the back for every sleep, the wrap snug at the chest but loose at the hips, and a firm plan to stop as soon as rolling attempts begin. It helps to think of swaddling as a comfort tool rather than a safety device. A swaddle does not make sleep safer on its own, and a poorly done one can add risk. If your baby consistently hates being wrapped, you lose nothing by skipping it. Feeding, rocking, white noise, and skin to skin contact can do similar calming work.

How to swaddle, step by step

Lay a thin blanket on a flat surface like a diamond and fold the top corner down about a hand's width. Place your baby on their back with the shoulders just below the fold. Gently straighten the left arm at the side or bend it across the chest, then bring the left side of the blanket over that arm and the chest and tuck it under the right side of the back. Fold the bottom corner up loosely over the feet, leaving plenty of room for the legs. Finally, do the same with the right arm, bring the remaining side of the blanket across the chest, and tuck it under the left side. The face and head must stay completely uncovered, with the fabric no higher than the shoulders.

The right tightness has a simple test: the wrap should be snug enough across the arms and chest that it cannot work loose during sleep, yet you should still be able to slide two to three fingers flat between the fabric and your baby's chest. Loose fabric near the face is the bigger danger, so err on the side of a secure chest wrap and a roomy bottom. Arms can go in or out. Arms wrapped down or across the chest calm the startle reflex best for most newborns, while wrapping under the armpits with arms free works well for babies who fight the wrap or who are getting close to the transition out.

Keep the hips loose

A swaddle that presses the legs straight down and together puts steady pressure on hip joints that are still soft and forming. Over weeks, that pressure can contribute to hip dysplasia, where the ball of the hip does not sit deeply in its socket. Hip healthy swaddling avoids this: from the hips down, the wrap stays loose enough that your baby can bend the knees and let the legs fall open into their natural frog position. If you use a swaddle sack, choose one with a roomy bag shape at the bottom rather than a tight pouch. Legs that can kick and flex freely inside the wrap are exactly what you want.

Some babies deserve extra attention on hips. If your baby was breech in the third trimester, or there is a family history of hip problems, mention it at the next checkup so the clinician can decide whether extra screening is useful. Between visits, contact your care team if you notice uneven thigh creases, one leg that seems shorter, a hip that clicks or clunks, or a leg your baby moves less than the other. Routine newborn and well child visits already include hip checks, so most concerns are caught early. Swaddling with loose hips is not the problem; the goal is simply to avoid adding pressure while the joints mature.

Safety rules for every swaddled sleep

Place a swaddled baby on the back for every sleep, at night and for naps. A wrapped baby who tips onto the stomach cannot push up or free the arms, which is why side and stomach positions are off limits and why rolling ends swaddling completely. If you ever find your swaddled baby on their side or stomach, return them to their back right away and treat that sleep as the end of swaddling, starting that same day. Check the wrap each time you lay your baby down: chest snug, hips loose, face clear, fabric below the shoulders. The sleep space itself should stay bare, with the swaddle as the only layer around your baby. If someone else puts your baby to sleep, a grandparent or a sitter, walk them through these rules once rather than assuming they know them.

Use one thin, breathable blanket or a swaddle sack sized for your baby's current weight, never two layers of wrapping. Skip weighted swaddles and weighted sleep sacks entirely; the American Academy of Pediatrics advises against weighted products for infant sleep. The swaddle itself counts as a layer, so one quick overheating check is enough: feel the back of the neck or the chest, and remove a layer if the skin feels hot or sweaty. If your baby was born early or has a medical condition, ask your care team before swaddling, since the advice can differ.

When to stop, and how to make the change

Stop swaddling at the very first sign your baby is trying to roll, not after the first successful roll. Early signs include rocking onto one side, lifting the hips and twisting, or repeatedly working an arm free overnight. Some babies show these attempts around 8 weeks, and pediatric guidance suggests stopping by about 2 months of age for most babies rather than waiting to be surprised. Every baby moves at their own pace, so watch behavior more than the calendar. It can help to note the date you first see rolling practice, in the BeMama app or anywhere you keep baby notes, so both parents make the change on the same night.

The transition works best in small steps. Start with one arm out of the swaddle for a few nights, then both arms out, then move to a sleep sack, a wearable blanket that keeps warmth without restricting the arms. Expect two or three unsettled nights at each step; startle wakes usually fade within a week or two as your baby learns to sleep with free arms. Keep everything else the same: back sleeping, a bare sleep space, and your usual wind down routine. If sleep falls apart for more than a couple of weeks, or your baby seems distressed rather than just adjusting, bring it up with your pediatrician.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Place a baby on their back for every sleep on a firm, flat, separate sleep surface with no pillows, loose bedding, positioners, or soft objects. Room sharing is recommended, but room sharing is different from sharing an adult bed, sofa, or chair.

Dress the baby for the room and avoid overheating or weighted sleep products. Swaddling does not make an unsafe sleep surface safe and should stop when a baby shows signs of trying to roll.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to coordinate sleep times and notice routine changes. Sleep totals cannot assess sleep safety or explain why a baby is unusually sleepy.

When to seek help

Seek prompt advice if a newborn is difficult to wake, feeds poorly, or has breathing or colour changes. Never use an inclined product, sofa, armchair, or car seat as a routine sleep space.

Sources and further reading

  • Public Health Agency of Canada — Safe Sleep for Your Baby
  • Health Canada — Dressing your baby for sleep

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Swaddle snug across the arms and chest, loose around the hips, with the face always uncovered.
  • Place a swaddled baby on their back for every sleep, never on the side or stomach.
  • Use one thin blanket or a correctly sized swaddle sack, and skip weighted products entirely.
  • Stop swaddling at the very first sign of trying to roll, often by around 2 months.
  • Transition gradually: one arm out for a few nights, then both, then a sleep sack.

Frequently asked questions

Is it safe to swaddle a newborn at night?

Yes, swaddling a newborn at night is considered safe when the baby sleeps on the back, the wrap is snug at the chest but loose at the hips, and the face stays fully uncovered. Use a single thin blanket or a correctly sized swaddle sack, and keep the rest of the sleep space bare. The same rules apply to naps. Stop night swaddling at the first sign of attempting to roll.

When should you stop swaddling?

Stop swaddling at the very first sign your baby tries to roll, which often appears around 8 weeks; pediatric guidance recommends stopping by about 2 months of age for most babies. Waiting for a full roll is waiting too long, because a swaddled baby who lands face down cannot push up or use the arms. Watch for side rocking, hip lifting, and arms working free, then start the transition to a sleep sack.

Should baby's arms be in or out of the swaddle?

Either can be safe; arms in, held straight down or bent across the chest, calms the startle reflex best for most newborns. Arms out, with the wrap under the armpits, suits babies who fight the swaddle or who are getting close to rolling. Many families use arms out as the first step of the transition. Whatever you choose, keep the fabric below the shoulders and away from the face.

How tight should a swaddle be?

A swaddle should be snug across the arms and chest but leave room to slide two to three flat fingers between the fabric and your baby's chest. Below the waist it should be loose, with space for the knees to bend and the legs to fall open. A wrap that restricts breathing or forces the legs straight is too tight, and one that can unravel near the face is too loose.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
